text: An AFTER trigger runs once the change already happened. An INSTEAD OF trigger is fundamentally different — it fires in place of the triggering insert, update, or delete. The real operation never happens at all unless the trigger body performs it itself.

Trigger on some view, instead of insert, as begin — and then the comment says it all: the real insert goes here, and if you skip it, nothing gets written anywhere. Inserted and deleted are still available inside, holding what would have been written.

The classic use case: EmployeeDirectory, a view joining Person and Employee. SQL Server can't update a two-table view directly, because it has no way to know which table a given column belongs to. So the trigger body does the routing by hand — first name and last name go to Person, job title goes to Employee — two separate updates, each reading from inserted.

That's the whole reason this exists: a multi-table view SQL Server can't guess the routing for. You write the routing logic once, inside the trigger, and from then on the view behaves as if it were directly updatable.
That closes out triggers. Next lesson, and the last one in this chapter, covers table-valued parameters — passing a whole batch of rows into a stored procedure in a single call.
